To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the scale elasticities of the network technology and the sub-technological frontiers are all less than unity, and, therefore, the network is characterized by decreasing returns to scale.

(1) the two approaches, based on the network technology construct with allocative inefficiency and independent sub-technologies, yield similar results; (2) there is a strong evidence of scale economies in both the sub-techno-logies and the network technology; and (3) the scale economies are more pronounced in the sub-technology of production than the sub-technology that transforms the raw materials into the final product.

(i) the network efficiency is the product of two sub-network efficiencies, (ii) the sub-network efficiency is the product two sub-technologies efficiencies, (iii) the scale efficiency is the ratio of the sub-network efficiencies, and (iv) the scale efficiency can be decomposed into the product of the scale efficiencies of the two sub-technological frontiers, which is a ratio of the sub-technological efficiencies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (i) What are the sources of inefficiencies of the network technology and the sub-technological inefficiencies?
the estimation of scale elasticity in two interdependent sub-stage technologies of a network production technology.

the decomposition of technical efficiency and scale elasticities of a network technology into the efficiencies of the sub-technological components, and the interdependence of the sub-technology components.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the two approaches yield different network efficiencies and scale elasticity measures, and the policy implications drawn from them are different.
the first approach is more suitable for a network technology with allocative inefficiency and the second approach is more suitable when allocative inefficiency is not present.
the first approach is more suitable when the network technology is characterized by allocative inefficiency and the second is more suitable when it is not.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the network efficiency of the first approach is decomposed into two components, namely, the technical efficiency of the network technology and the technical efficiency of one of the sub-technology.

the network technology approach provides a more accurate estimate of scale economies for the entire network technology, whereas the independent sub-technology approach provides a more precise estimate of scale economies in the sub-technology front.
the scale efficiency of a network technology is the weighted sum of scale efficiencies of its sub-technological components.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the two-stage network technology, as proposed by Kao and Hwaing (2011) is not a generalization of the single network technology.
the scale efficiency of sub-technologies is not necessarily the same as the scale efficiency of the network technology.
a single network technology is not adequate to decompose technical efficiency and scale efficiency of a multi-stage production system.
